title: India Just Told WhatsApp to Freeze Its Biggest Privacy Update. Half a Billion Users Are in Limbo.
excerpt: New Delhi has given Meta three days to explain how its username feature won't become a playground for scammers — or face regulatory action
body:
WhatsApp was supposed to give its users something they'd wanted for years: a username, so you could message someone without handing over your phone number. The feature had already begun a phased global rollout, and Indian users were reserving their preferred handles.

Then New Delhi pulled the handbrake.

In a letter dated July 1, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology directed Meta to freeze the username rollout in India — the platform's largest market, with more than 500 million users — and explain within three days why regulatory action should not be initiated. Until consultations with the government are complete, the feature cannot go live.

## The Government's Concern: Anonymity as a Weapon

India's objection is blunt: usernames could supercharge the very scams the country is already struggling to contain.

The IT ministry's letter flagged specific risks — phishing attacks, digital arrest scams, financial fraud, and identity impersonation. Officials warned that usernames resembling those of banks, government agencies, or well-known individuals could be weaponised to deceive users who wouldn't notice a subtle misspelling.

The intervention comes weeks after India temporarily blocked Telegram over anonymity concerns, and follows years of clashes with Elon Musk's X over content-takedown orders. For New Delhi, the pattern is clear: platforms that make it harder to identify bad actors will face pushback.


![Information Technology — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/f/f3/CSIRO_ScienceImage_8130_The_computer_lab_on_RV_Southern_Surveyor.jpg)



> **"An optional "username key" adds a second layer: both the username and key would be required before a new conversation could begin."**



"This could materially increase online fraud," the ministry said in its letter, according to Reuters, which reviewed the document.

## What WhatsApp Actually Built

The username feature, which Meta announced earlier this week, would let users create a unique handle — up to 35 characters — and optionally share it instead of their phone number. The company positioned it as a privacy upgrade, particularly useful for group chats, business interactions, and connecting with strangers without exposing personal contact details.

WhatsApp added several safeguards. There is no public directory of usernames — you'd need to know someone's exact handle to message them. An optional "username key" adds a second layer: both the username and key would be required before a new conversation could begin. And the platform said it had already reserved usernames for public figures, government entities, celebrities, and verified Meta accounts to prevent impersonation.

"We've announced the option for people to reserve their preferred username on WhatsApp," a Meta spokesperson said, emphasising that the feature is not yet live. "The ability to use a username is not yet live and will roll out slowly later this year."

Lookalike variations of well-known names have also been blocked from registration, the company added. Automated systems detect suspicious behaviour and cap how many new people an account can contact through usernames.


## The Telegram Precedent


![New Delhi — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fe/Forecourt%2C_Rashtrapati_Bhavan_-_1.jpg/3840px-Forecourt%2C_Rashtrapati_Bhavan_-_1.jpg)


India's move is not without context. Last month, the government temporarily blocked Telegram after determining that the app's anonymous username system had been exploited to distribute illegal content, coordinate financial fraud, and run impersonation schemes. The block was lifted after Telegram agreed to cooperate with Indian law enforcement on content moderation.

The WhatsApp intervention follows the same logic: if a feature enables anonymity, New Delhi wants to vet it before 500 million users start using it.

But the comparison is imperfect. Telegram's usernames are fully public and searchable — anyone can find anyone. WhatsApp's system is designed to be the opposite: no directory, no search, no discovery. You only reach someone if you already have their exact username.

## What This Means for Users

For now, nothing changes for WhatsApp users in India. The app continues to function as it always has — phone-number-based contacts, end-to-end encryption, group chats. Users who reserved usernames during the early rollout will keep those reservations, but the feature cannot be activated until the government review concludes.

The three-day deadline for Meta's response expires on July 4. If the company fails to satisfy the ministry's concerns, India could take regulatory action under the Information Technology Act — a prospect that would force Meta to choose between compliance and pushing back against what critics see as an expanding government appetite for platform control.

For the Indian diaspora, the stakes are personal. WhatsApp is not just a messaging app in India — it is the primary channel through which families stay connected across continents, businesses coordinate supply chains, and communities organise everything from weddings to mutual aid. Any restriction on the platform's evolution, even a temporary one, ripples outward to every NRI household that depends on it.

The question now is whether Meta's safeguards will be enough for a government that has shown little patience for Silicon Valley's "move fast" instincts — and whether India's 500 million WhatsApp users will ever get to message someone without first sharing the most personal identifier they have.

nri_angle: NRIs depend on WhatsApp more than almost any other app to stay connected with family in India — any feature change or government restriction directly affects how the diaspora communicates.
